title: test-0074-SCI-BIO-PLANTNUTRITION
passage: Many people mistakenly believe that plants simply suck up their food from the soil through their roots, much like we drink through a straw. In reality, plants are autotrophs that manufacture their own food using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. While roots do absorb water and minerals, they do not take in food. Furthermore, some students think that non-green leaves cannot perform photosynthesis. However, leaves of other colors also contain chlorophyll, which is masked by larger amounts of other pigments. Another common error is the idea that insectivorous plants, like the pitcher plant, trap insects because they cannot perform photosynthesis. These plants actually live in soil poor in nitrogen, so they consume insects specifically to obtain the nitrogen they need to grow. Finally, some believe that Rhizobium bacteria are harmful pests that infect plants. In truth, these bacteria live in a symbiotic relationship within the root nodules of leguminous plants, converting atmospheric nitrogen into a usable form for the plant, while the plant provides them with shelter and nutrients. This partnership is mutually beneficial, not parasitic. Understanding these processes helps us appreciate how plants sustain themselves and interact with other organisms in their environment.
summary: Many people think plants just take food from the soil through their roots like we take food from a straw. In fact, these bacteria live in a symbiotic relationship inside the root nodules of leguminous plants, helping the plant grow by converting atmospheric nitrogen into a usable form.
